stem.text: Alleles are alternative forms of a gene. For example, there may be a dominant allele, T, and a recessive allele, t, at the same gene locus.
The relative frequency of each allele of a gene in a population can change over time due to factors such as selection, genetic drift and the bottleneck effect.
Fig. 4.1 shows the relative frequency of the T allele in a population of 50 individuals over 20 generations.

At generation 0, the number of T alleles and the number of t alleles in the population was equal, so the relative frequency of each allele was 0.5. The relative frequencies of the two alleles of the gene add up to 1.

explanation.text: Drift is a chance change in allele frequencies and has greater relative effects in small populations. A founder event or bottleneck samples only part of the original gene pool.
